subtype: Fear of standing before the class [Actor]
passage: Sangeeta, come closer. I'm your Ammamma Manjula, and when I was nine I had to recite a poem in front of the whole class. My heart went thump-thump like a drum, my mouth turned dry as chalk, and I forgot every line. I was sure every eye was laughing at me. My teacher did not scold. She said, "Tell it to the tulsi plant this evening." So I did, three nights. Then I said it to my friend Leela, then to the teacher alone. When I stood up in class again my voice shook, but I reached the last line. Nobody laughed. Leela clapped first.

qa.q: What did the teacher tell Manjula to do first?
qa.a: She told Manjula to tell the poem to the tulsi plant that evening.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when she first stood in front of the class?
qa.a: Terrified, with a racing heart and a dry mouth, sure that every eye was laughing.

qa.q: What helped Manjula reach the last line the second time?
qa.a: Practising the poem in small, safe steps: to the plant, then to Leela, then to the teacher alone.

qa.q: How did Leela seem to feel about Manjula's recitation?
qa.a: Leela was supportive and proud, shown by clapping first when nobody laughed.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a child's racing heart, dry mouth and forgotten lines, eased by gentle repeated practice.

subtype: Fear of standing before the class [Actor]
passage: The assembly bell would ring in five minutes, and Madhav was next to say his poem in front of the whole school. His heart was racing, his mouth felt dry, and the words had vanished. In the corridor Francis Sir saw him gripping the paper. "Say the first line to me. Only me." Madhav whispered it. "Now the second, to the wall." He said all four lines to the wall while the noisy line of children passed. On the stage his voice shook and he forgot the third line. He looked at Francis Sir, who mouthed the first word. Madhav finished. Nobody was laughing. A few children were fidgeting with their shoes.

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the assembly bell?
qa.a: There were five minutes left.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling in the corridor while gripping the paper?
qa.a: Nervous and scared of forgetting, with a racing heart and a dry mouth.

qa.q: What did Francis Sir do that made a difference?
qa.a: He had Madhav say the lines quietly to him and to the wall, and then mouthed the first word when Madhav forgot the third line.

qa.q: What were the children in the audience paying attention to?
qa.a: Most were not judging Madhav; a few were fidgeting with their shoes, which suggests they were busy with themselves.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild's racing heart and forgotten lines before reciting, eased by low-stakes practice.

subtype: Fear of standing before the class [Actor]
passage:
It had rained all night, so the assembly moved into the small hall, and the microphone died.
Harsha stood at the front with his poem. His heart was banging. His mouth felt like cotton. He said the first line. Then nothing. The second line had gone.
A boy giggled. Harsha's face burned. Gautam sir quietly walked up and said the first word of the line. Harsha finished, too fast and too soft, and ran back to his place.
That week Gautam sir asked him to say the poem only to him, in the empty classroom. Then to three friends at lunch. Then to his little sister at home. On Monday he said it to the class from his own desk. His hands still shook a little. He didn't forget a single line.

qa.q: Why did the assembly move into the small school hall?
qa.a: It had rained all night.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when the second line went?
qa.a: Harsha was frightened and ashamed; his heart was banging, his mouth was dry and his face burned when a boy giggled.

qa.q: Which of Gautam sir's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Having Harsha say the poem to one person, then three friends, then his sister, because small, safe practice made the class feel less scary.

qa.q: How might Gautam sir have felt watching Harsha freeze?
qa.a: Gautam sir was probably concerned and kind, stepping up quietly to give one word rather than letting Harsha struggle alone.

grounding: Shows a child who freezes while reciting before a crowd, and gentle practice in small, safe settings that makes it less frightening.

subtype: Fear of standing before the class [Actor]
passage:
Damini's science project was a water cycle model: a shoebox, cotton clouds and blue cellophane. On Tuesday she had to explain it to her class in their Kolkata school.
When she stood up, her heart raced so fast she could hear it. She said, "This is the water cycle," and her mind went white. Thirty faces. She was sure every one of them thought she was stupid. She sat down.
At home she didn't want dinner. Her father, Kishore, didn't push. Later he lined up her soft toys on the bed. "Tell them," he said. She giggled and told them. The next evening he called in the two children from next door, and her voice wobbled only once.
On Friday Damini tried again, looking at her friend in the second row.

qa.q: What did Damini use to make the clouds?
qa.a: She made them with cotton clouds.

qa.q: What was Damini sure of when she faced thirty faces?
qa.a: Damini was frightened and sure every one of them thought she was stupid.

qa.q: How did Kishore help Damini get ready for Friday?
qa.a: Kishore let her practise first with soft toys and then with two neighbour children, small safe audiences before the class.

qa.q: What was that evening like for Kishore?
qa.a: Kishore probably felt worried when Damini did not want dinner, but he chose patience over pushing.

grounding: Illustrates a child whose racing heart and blank mind in front of the class ease with gentle, low-stakes practice at home.

subtype: Fear of standing before the class [Actor]
passage:
"Joseph sir, can I not do show-and-tell tomorrow?"
"Why not, Nazia?"
"My heart goes boom boom. My mouth goes dry. And everyone looks at me."
"What were you going to show?"
"My Nani's old camera."
"What if you tell it just to me first? Right now, at lunch. The class is outside."
Nazia held up the camera. "This is my Nani's camera. It is older than my mummy. You look in here and press this…"
"And then?"
"I forgot."
"That's okay. Take a breath. What happens when you press it?"
"It goes click and the film goes round!"
"Good. Tomorrow, tell it to me and Ruhi and Ayaan at lunch. On Friday, maybe the class."
Nazia thought. "Okay. But you sit in the front."

qa.q: Whose camera was Nazia going to show?
qa.a: My Nani's old camera.

qa.q: How does Nazia describe feeling about show-and-tell?
qa.a: Nazia feels scared and nervous: a heart that goes boom boom, a dry mouth and everyone looking.

qa.q: What step-by-step plan does Joseph sir offer?
qa.a: First tell it only to him at lunch, then to two friends the next day, and maybe the class on Friday.

qa.q: How does Joseph sir respond when Nazia forgets?
qa.a: Joseph sir stays calm and encouraging, telling Nazia it's okay and asking a simple question to help Nazia remember.

grounding: Shows a child afraid of speaking before the class and a teacher who offers gentle, repeated practice in small settings.

subtype: Fear of standing before the class [Actor]
passage: I'm Keerthana. In class five, Miss Ritu asked me to read my rain story aloud to the class. I stood up and my heart banged so hard I thought everyone could hear it. My mouth went dry like chalk. I looked at the page and the words swam. I read the first line, then lost my place, and somebody at the back giggled. I sat down with my face burning, sure the whole class would remember it forever. Miss Ritu didn't make me finish. That week she let me read the story just to her, at lunch. Then to her and my friend Anu. Then to four people on the steps. The next month I read a new story to the whole class. My heart still banged, but I got to the end.

qa.q: What story did Keerthana have to read aloud?
qa.a: The rain story.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel sitting down after the giggle?
qa.a: Keerthana felt embarrassed and scared, face burning, sure the whole class would remember it forever.

qa.q: What did Miss Ritu do that made reading aloud less frightening?
qa.a: She let Keerthana practise in small, safe steps, first to her alone, then with Anu, then to four people, before the whole class.

qa.q: How might Miss Ritu have felt watching Keerthana sit down?
qa.a: Miss Ritu was probably concerned and kind, which is why she didn't force Keerthana to finish and planned small practice sessions instead.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild whose heart races and mouth goes dry reading in front of the class, and who grows braver through gentle practice in small groups.
